meaning: The beloved of Kṛṣṇa, chief of the gopīs (from √rādh, 'to succeed, accomplish')

pronunciation.approximation: RAH-dhah — both a's are long; the dh is a single aspirated sound, not two letters.
pronunciation.note: Sanskrit Rādhā derives from √rādh, "to prosper, accomplish, propitiate" — Monier-Williams glosses the word as prosperity and success, and records her celestial namesake: the nakshatra Viśākhā is also called Rādhā. The restoration Rādhā keeps both long vowels exactly where the Sanskrit puts them; the ASCII "Radha" flattens the two syllables the tradition holds long. Tier-1 by rule: two macrons preserved.

domains.title: The Beloved of Vraja
domains.subtitle: The Rāsa Dance, the Gītagovinda, and the Theology of Longing
domains.lead: Rādhā is the chief of the gopīs and the supreme beloved of Krishna: the village girl of Vraja whom the poets and the theologians raised, century by century, until she stood as goddess beside — and, for her devotees, above — the god she loves.

cards.name: The Rāsa Circle
cards.desc: The autumn full-moon dance of the Bhāgavata's tenth book — Krishna multiplied among the gopīs.

cards.name: The Gītagovinda
cards.desc: Jayadeva's twelfth-century song-cycle — the poem that taught India to sing her name beside Mādhava's.

cards.name: Rādhā-kuṇḍa
cards.desc: Her bathing-pool below Govardhan — for the Gauḍīyas the most sacred water on earth.

cards.name: Varṣāṇā (Barsana)
cards.desc: Her village on the ridge — the hilltop temples where Holi is played in her honor every spring.

symbols.name: The golden lotus
symbols.meaning: Her complexion and her purity: gaurī, the golden one, the lotus of the Yamunā's bank

symbols.name: The kadamba tryst-tree

symbols.name: The cry "Rādhe"
symbols.meaning: The vocative that outranks every title: in Braj her name is itself a blessing

mythology.lead: Rādhā's mythology is the rarest kind: a figure the early texts leave unnamed, whom poetry and devotion then build, line by line, into the measure of divine love itself.

myths.title: The Unnamed Beloved
myths.text: The Bhāgavata Purāṇa tells the rāsa-līlā across five chapters of its tenth book — the autumn full-moon night on the Yamunā's bank, Krishna's flute emptying the village, the dance in which he multiplies himself among the gopīs — and never once speaks her name. Yet one verse (10.30.28) says of one gopī, anayārādhito nūnaṃ bhagavān hariḥ: "surely the Lord was perfectly worshipped by her." The great commentators hear the name hidden in the verb: ārādhitaḥ, worshipped — Rādhā. Her devotees have ever since read the whole book as her portrait, unsigned.

myths.title: The Poem That Crowned Her
myths.text: In the twelfth century Jayadeva wrote the Gītagovinda, and the unsigned portrait got its signature. His aṣṭapadīs — songs in eights — stage the whole drama of separation and union: the go-between urging Rādhā through the spring night to the tryst, Krishna begging her foot on his head, the refrain rādhā-mādhavayor jayati yamunā-kūle raḥaḥ-kelayaḥ — "the secret love-play of Rādhā and Mādhava triumphs on the Yamunā's bank." The poem was taken into temple liturgy — it is sung before Jagannātha at Puri to this day — and Rādhā's name became inseparable from the god's.

myths.title: From Beloved to Goddess
myths.text: The later purāṇas complete the ascent. The Brahma-vaivarta Purāṇa makes Rādhā the prakṛti itself — the primal nature from whom all goddesses proceed, Krishna's own other half, without whom he is not merely lonely but incomplete. What the Bhāgavata hinted and Jayadeva sang, the sectarian texts systematized: the cowherd girl of Vraja is the very power by which the divine loves, and being loved is shown to be a divine attribute, not a divine accident.

myths.title: The Mood the Lord Borrowed
myths.text: The Gauḍīya theologians gave the ascent its final form: Rādhā is Krishna's hlādinī-śakti, his bliss-potency, and her love is the one thing in existence he does not already possess. Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja's Caitanya-caritāmṛta explains the Golden Avatar by her: Krishna, curious what she feels in loving him, takes her mood and her golden complexion and is born as Caitanya. Devotion does not merely reach God here; God is defined by the reach of devotion. Her festival, Rādhāṣṭamī, falls on the eighth of Bhādrapada's bright fortnight, fifteen days after his birthday — her own day, in her own right.

lore.syncretism: Her worship organizes whole sampradāyas: the Nimbārkas adore the yugala, the divine couple, as one; the Rādhā-vallabhīs of Hita Harivaṃśa's line put her name first and her temple at the center of Vrindavan; the Gauḍīyas approach Krishna through her maidservants. Comparatists have set the Gītagovinda beside the Song of Songs as bridal mysticism's two great poems, and the parallel holds better than most: both traditions insist that longing is a form of knowledge. Monier-Williams records her homonym in the sky — the nakshatra Viśākhā bears the name Rādhā — as if the calendar itself had enrolled her.
lore.culturalLegacy: Rādhā is one of the most-spoken divine names on earth: "Rādhe Rādhe" is the everyday greeting of Braj, her Rādhāṣṭamī fills Varṣāṇā's lanes, and the spring Holi of Barsana — the Lāthmār Holi where the women playfully beat the men of Krishna's village — is broadcast worldwide. Kangra and Pahari painters made her longing the face of Indian miniature art; Sūrdās and the bhakti poets sang her in every northern tongue. She gave the tradition its most radical sentence: the devotee, not the deity, is the measure of the divine.
lore.extendedMeditation: Rādhā is the proof that devotion is not a means but an end: she does not worship in order to obtain, she loves — and the tradition watched that love until it concluded that God must be made of the same substance. Every act of care done without calculation walks in her rāsa circle. Her question to the powerful is her question to Krishna: what is all your power for, if not this?
lore.archaeology: Her monuments are the sacred geography of Braj: Varṣāṇā (Barsana), her village, crowned by the Lārlījī temple on its ridge; Govardhan hill, around which pilgrims still circle barefoot; and Rādhā-kuṇḍa, her bathing-pool, restored and excavated in the sixteenth century under Raghunātha dāsa Gosvāmin and venerated by the Gauḍīyas as the holiest water in existence. The Rādhāvallabha temple in Vrindavan anchors her own sampradāya, and the illustrated Gītagovinda manuscripts — palm-leaf and paper, from Odisha to the Punjab Hills — are among the glories of Indian painting.
